subject: Copywriting
title: Reason-Why Advertising
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Reason-Why Advertising.

hook.text: In 1904, John E. Kennedy told an ad exec that advertising was 'salesmanship in print.' Three words changed the field.

buildup.text: Before Kennedy, ads were decorative announcements. He argued every ad should give a reason to buy.

discovery.text: Claude Hopkins took it further. He tested headlines, tracked coupons, and measured results obsessively.

twist.text: Artists hated reason-why. They wanted beautiful ads. Hopkins wanted ads that sold. Sales always won.

climax.text: Hopkins' book 'Scientific Advertising' is still required reading. Data-driven copy started in 1923.

punchline.text: Three words: salesmanship in print. Copy got a purpose.

quiz.question: Who defined advertising as 'salesmanship in print'?

details.summary: Reason-why advertising, championed by John E. Kennedy and Claude Hopkins, held that every ad must give the consumer a specific reason to buy. Instead of vague claims, ads presented factual arguments: ingredients, processes, tests, and guarantees. This rational approach dominated early 20th...
details.whyItMatters: Reason-why advertising established the principle that copy must persuade with evidence. In an era of emotional marketing, understanding when facts sell better than feelings remains a vital skill.
takeaways: Every ad must give a specific, factual reason to buy the product
Kennedy defined advertising as 'salesmanship in print'
Evidence-based copy built trust in an era of patent medicine snake oil

faq.question: What is reason-why advertising?
faq.answer: It is copy that presents a specific, logical argument for why the reader should buy. Instead of 'Best soap in the world,' a reason-why ad says: 'Made with palm and olive oils, aged for three months, tested in 47 hospitals.' Facts replace puffery.

faq.question: Is reason-why advertising still relevant?
faq.answer: Very much so. B2B marketing, technology products, and high-consideration purchases still rely heavily on factual, evidence-based copy. The approach is also fundamental to direct-response advertising, landing pages, and comparison marketing.
